extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of literature/philosophy (readers of Montaigne)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting practical maxims and prescriptive observations from Montaigne's essay on bodily life, pleasure, and moderation; the page is a literary/philosophical essay rather than a formal guideline. Useful for readers studying Renaissance essayistic advice about living.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value the present and avoid chasing vain hopes
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who pass over the present and that which they possess, to wait on hope, and for shadows and vain images which fancy puts before them; 'The fruit and end of their pursuit is to pursue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns against sacrificing current life and possessions for speculative future gains; the pursuit becomes self-perpetuating and hollow (example: Alexander 'the end of his labour was to labour'). Prefer attending to and enjoying what exists now rather than endless striving after illusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept and enjoy natural bodily pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I love life and cultivate it... I do not desire it should be without the necessity of eating and drinking... I accept kindly, and with gratitude, what nature has done for me; am well pleased with it, and proud of it. A man does wrong to that great and omnipotent giver to refuse, annul, or disfigure his gift.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bodily needs and pleasures (eating, drinking, sexual appetite, etc.) are natural and good; refusing or disfiguring them is ungrateful and wrong. Montaigne rejects extreme denial of natural faculties and endorses a thankful, measured enjoyment of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer solid, human, and modest philosophy suited to one's manners
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Of philosophical opinions, I preferably embrace those that are most solid, that is to say, the most human and most our own: my discourse is, suitable to my manners, low and humble.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy should be practical, humane, and compatible with ordinary life and manners. Avoid philosophies that elevate themselves into fantastical extremes or divorce the human from the earthly; value modest, applicable wisdom over abstruse or pretentious systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value mental pleasures while maintaining temperance for bodily pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates 'values, as he ought, bodily pleasure; but he prefers that of the mind... Temperance with him is the moderatrix, not the adversary of pleasure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mental pleasures have more force, constancy, variety, and dignity, but bodily pleasures need not be rejected—temperance should moderate them. The guideline is to prioritize intellectual enjoyment without making bodily pleasure an enemy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate the nature of things and act according to what nature requires
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Intrandum est in rerum naturam, et penitus, quid ea postulet, pervidendum.' — A man must search into the nature of things, and fully examine what she requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should examine the underlying nature and requirements of things and let that understanding guide action. This supports aligning conduct with natural conditions rather than abstract ideals detached from reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate body and mind; do not despise necessary actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne argues against separating divine/mental from earthly/body: 'Let the mind rouse and quicken the heaviness of the body, and the body stay and fix the levity of the soul.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than dismembering life into superior/inferior parts, cultivate a reciprocal relationship between mind and body. Necessary bodily actions are not less worthy—marry pleasure with necessity for a balanced life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat present life as a moral commission and care for the embodied self
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In this present that God has made us, there is nothing unworthy our care; we stand accountable... the Creator has seriously and strictly prescribed it to us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caring for one's present, embodied life is a duty; neglecting the body's needs or despising earthly life is improper. Montaigne frames attention to ordinary life as a moral responsibility rather than mere indulgence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not sacrifice immediate, ordinary pleasures to abstract meditation
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne counsels asking people what whimsies distracted them from a good meal and finds those meditations often less worthwhile than the meal; 'his discourses and notions are not worth the worst mess there.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive abstraction or speculative ecstasy that causes one to miss simple enjoyments (like a meal) is criticized. Practical, immediate experiences often outweigh remote intellectual fancies; keep meditation commensurate with daily life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extreme asceticism and transcendental affectations
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is folly; instead of transforming themselves into angels, they transform themselves into beasts.' Montaigne rejects ecstasies and communications with demons, extreme self-denial, and excessive elevation above human condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extremes of mystical or ascetic practice that deny humanity often degrade rather than elevate. Maintain human proportion and avoid affectations that remove one from ordinary, humane comportment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live moderately within the common human model; favour sociable, pleasant old age
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The fairest lives, in my opinion, are those which regularly accommodate themselves to the common and human model without miracle, without extravagance... Old age stands a little in need of a more gentle treatment... let it be gay and sociable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a moderate, ordinary life rather than extraordinary extremes. In aging, favour gentle, sociable pleasures—avoid making old age miserable through needless austerity or theatrical severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: A well-governed stomach is a great part of liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: (Editor’s bookmark aphorism quoted in text) 'A well-governed stomach is a great part of liberty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical health and sensible management of bodily needs (especially eating) are foundational to freedom and wellbeing; bodily regulation supports liberty of mind and action.
